title: Plant Science & Genetics
summary: Breeding better crops with genetics and statistics. Heritability and the breeder's equation are the threshold: they turn 'pick the best plants' into a prediction of how much the next generation will improve, and why the environment can undo it.
sources: Falconer & Mackay: Introduction to Quantitative Genetics
Acquaah: Principles of Plant Genetics and Breeding
Taiz, Zeiger et al.: Plant Physiology and Development
Visscher, Hill, Wray: Heritability in the genomics era (2008)

nodes.label: Plant Cells & Growth
nodes.summary: Cell walls, vacuoles, meristems and hormones (auxin, gibberellin) that shape growth.
nodes.outcome: Explain how auxin causes a shoot to bend toward light.
nodes.check: A shoot bends toward a window. What does auxin do to cause it?
nodes.answer: Auxin moves to the shaded side and makes those cells elongate more, bending the shoot toward the light.

nodes.label: Photosynthesis & Yield
nodes.summary: Light capture, carbon fixation (C3 vs C4) and how canopy architecture limits crop yield.
nodes.outcome: Compare C3 and C4 crops in hot, dry conditions.
nodes.check: Why do C4 crops like maize do better than C3 crops in hot, sunny conditions?
nodes.answer: They concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO, which suppresses photorespiration.

nodes.label: Inheritance in Crops
nodes.summary: Mendelian traits, linkage and recombination in crop pedigrees and crosses.
nodes.outcome: Use recombination frequency to estimate map distance.
nodes.check: Two genes recombine in 10% of offspring. How far apart are they on the genetic map?

nodes.label: Polyploidy
nodes.summary: Many crops (wheat, potato, strawberry) carry more than two genome copies, which changes inheritance ratios and vigour.
nodes.outcome: Explain why bread wheat is hexaploid and what that means for breeding.
nodes.check: How many sets of chromosomes does a hexaploid plant have?

nodes.label: Quantitative Genetics
nodes.summary: Yield, height and drought tolerance are controlled by many genes of small effect plus environment: P = G + E.
nodes.outcome: Partition phenotypic variance into genetic and environmental parts.
nodes.check: Why do most yield traits show a bell-shaped distribution rather than discrete classes?
nodes.answer: Many genes of small effect plus environmental variation add up to a continuous distribution.

nodes.label: Heritability & the Breeder's Equation
nodes.summary: Narrow-sense heritability h² is the share of variance due to additive genes. Response to selection R = h²S predicts the gain per generation.
nodes.outcome: Predict the response to selection with R = h²S.
nodes.check: Selected plants average 20 kg/ha above the population mean and h² = 0.3. Expected gain in the next generation?

nodes.label: "High heritability means genes fix the trait"
nodes.summary: Heritability describes a population in an environment, not an individual, and a highly heritable trait can still change a lot with the environment.
nodes.outcome: Explain why heritability is population- and environment-specific.
nodes.check: Height has high heritability. Does that mean better nutrition cannot make a population taller?
nodes.answer: No: heritability is about variation within a population in one environment; changing the environment can shift the whole population.

nodes.label: Genotype × Environment Interaction
nodes.summary: Varieties rank differently across locations and years, so trials must span environments.
nodes.outcome: Read a GxE plot and recommend varieties for target environments.
nodes.check: Variety A beats B at the wet site but B beats A at the dry site. What is this called?

nodes.label: Field Trial Design
nodes.summary: Replication, randomisation and blocking separate genetic differences from soil and weather noise.
nodes.outcome: Lay out a randomised complete block design for six varieties.
nodes.check: Why randomise variety positions within each block of a field trial?
nodes.answer: So soil gradients and other hidden field effects don't systematically favour one variety.

nodes.label: Molecular Markers & QTL Mapping
nodes.summary: DNA markers linked to genes let breeders locate quantitative trait loci and track them through crosses.
nodes.outcome: Interpret a QTL scan and choose markers for selection.
nodes.check: What does a QTL peak on a mapping plot indicate?
nodes.answer: A chromosome region associated with variation in the trait.

nodes.label: Marker-Assisted & Genomic Selection
nodes.summary: Select seedlings by DNA before the trait can be measured; genomic selection predicts breeding values from genome-wide markers.
nodes.outcome: Explain how genomic selection shortens the breeding cycle.
nodes.check: Why can genomic selection speed up breeding for a trait like yield?
nodes.answer: Plants can be selected from their DNA as seedlings, before costly field trials, shortening each cycle.

nodes.label: Gene Editing in Crops
nodes.summary: CRISPR knockouts and edits create traits like disease resistance without adding foreign DNA.
nodes.outcome: Describe how a CRISPR knockout creates a disease-resistant variety.
nodes.check: How can knocking a gene out make a plant more disease-resistant?
nodes.answer: Some pathogens need a host 'susceptibility' gene; removing it denies the pathogen what it needs (e.g. mlo resistance to powdery mildew).

nodes.label: "Eating GM food transfers its genes to you"
nodes.summary: All food contains DNA, which is digested; genes from food do not become part of the eater's genome.
nodes.outcome: Explain what happens to DNA in food.
nodes.check: Does eating a GM tomato put its genes into your cells?
nodes.answer: No: DNA in any food is broken down by digestion; it isn't incorporated into your genome.

nodes.label: High-Throughput Phenotyping
nodes.summary: Drones, imaging and sensors measure thousands of plots quickly; the bottleneck moves from genotyping to measuring traits.
nodes.outcome: Choose a sensor and index (e.g. NDVI) to measure crop vigour.
nodes.check: NDVI compares reflectance in which two bands?

nodes.label: Variety Release & Seed Systems
nodes.summary: Testing, registration, multiplication and farmer adoption: a variety only matters if farmers can get and grow it.
nodes.outcome: Plan the steps from an elite line to seed in farmers' hands.
nodes.check: Why might a high-yielding new variety fail to be adopted by farmers?
nodes.answer: If it lacks traits they value (taste, cooking quality, local adaptation), seed is unavailable or too costly, or it was never tested in their conditions.
